claims.text: Anthropic found a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on its internal research eval.
In the BrowseComp evaluation, token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance; token usage, number of tool calls, and model choice together explained 95%.
Upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 gave a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7.
Agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, so they need tasks valuable enough to justify the cost.

Anthropic's testing found multi-agent implementations typically use 3-10x more tokens than single-agent approaches for equivalent tasks, due to duplicated context, coordination messages, and summarizing results for handoffs.
Teams that built elaborate multi-agent systems with separate planning, execution, review, and iteration agents suffered lost context at each handoff and spent more tokens coordinating than executing.
The Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern: a lead agent analyzes the query, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents that search different aspects in parallel.
The LeadResearcher saves its plan to Memory because the context window is truncated if it exceeds 200,000 tokens.
After the research loop, a CitationAgent processes the documents and report to identify specific locations for citations.

Each subagent given to a lead agent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries; vague instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage' led to duplicated searches.
Scaling rules embedded in prompts: simple fact-finding uses 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research more than 10 subagents.
Early Research agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries, searched endlessly for nonexistent sources, and distracted each other with excessive updates.
Parallelization (lead spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel; subagents use 3+ tools in parallel) cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.
A tool-testing agent that rewrote flawed MCP tool descriptions produced a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents.
Multi-agent systems are a poor fit for tasks requiring a shared context or many inter-agent dependencies; most coding tasks have fewer parallelizable parts than research.
The Claude Agent SDK supports subagents, which enable parallelization and manage context by using isolated context windows and sending only relevant information back to the orchestrator.
The Claude Agent SDK's compact feature automatically summarizes previous messages as the context limit approaches, built on Claude Code's compact slash command.

The long-running harness uses an initializer agent in the first session to create an init.sh script, a claude-progress.txt log, and an initial git commit; subsequent coding agent sessions make incremental progress and leave structured updates.
Compaction alone was insufficient: agents tried to one-shot the app and ran out of context mid-feature, or later declared the job done prematurely after seeing progress.

The initializer wrote a feature list of over 200 features for the claude.ai clone, all initially marked failing; coding agents may only change the passes field, and JSON was chosen because the model is less likely to inappropriately overwrite JSON than Markdown.

Each coding session starts by running pwd, reading git logs and the progress file, choosing the highest-priority unfinished feature from the feature list, and running init.sh with a basic end-to-end test before new work.
Claude marked features complete without end-to-end testing until explicitly prompted to use browser automation (Puppeteer MCP); it could not see browser-native alert modals.

Context resets (clearing the context with a structured handoff) differ from compaction, which summarizes in place; Sonnet 4.5 showed 'context anxiety' strongly enough that compaction alone was insufficient, though resets add orchestration complexity, token overhead, and latency.
Opus 4.5 largely removed context anxiety, so a later planner-generator-evaluator harness dropped context resets and used one continuous session with the Claude Agent SDK's automatic compaction.
In the retro game maker comparison, the solo run took 20 minutes and cost $9 while the full three-agent harness took 6 hours and cost $200, but produced a working play mode the solo run lacked.
